title: Inside the Home Gym of 2 Elite Athletes
author: Emily LaPointe
text:
If you live in a climate that buries the roads for months at a time, an indoor trainer becomes a major part of preseason training. Just ask Haley Smith and Andrew L’Esperance. The two elite off-road racers—partners on and off the bike—have dialed their indoor setups and workouts for head-of-the-pack performance. At the center of it all are the Wahoo KICKR CORE 2 and the KICKR V6—trainers designed to guide athletes through indoor-to-outdoor transitions with smart features, connectivity, and accessories.

Haley Smith: My indoor workouts are very targeted and optimized: zero junk miles and a high degree of specificity. It’s really common for me to do a large volume of intensity work in a relatively short ride. Torque or muscular endurance work, threshold blocks, and over/unders are frequent indoor rides for me. The KICKR V6 and the ability to toggle between trainer settings on my head unit make it all possible. (Typically, I’m running the ELMNT Roam 3 .) I can adjust the trainer difficulty, turn erg mode on or off, and follow planned workouts right from the head unit without needing to fire up a third-party app. Wahoo plays nicely with third-party platforms, so I’ll often use those for variety and visual stimulus/boredom busters.

Andrew L’Esperance: Either a block of high zone 2, lactic threshold 1 (LT1) work, or a version of over/unders. For the high zone 2 work, I would do 20-to-30-minute blocks and four to eight repeats, depending on the time of year and length of workout. For over/unders, I start with one minute “over” and three minutes “under,” and adjust my recovery time and intensity based on the time of year and goal of the session.

Smith: The KICKR V6 is my favorite indoor training tool—it’s the main event! But a hugely underrated piece of equipment has to be the KICKR Desk . It’s one of those pieces that, before owning, I would have labeled as “nice to have but not necessary.” Now, I am totally dependent on it. Being able to roll the table back and forth and easily adjust the height makes trainer rides so much more enjoyable and practical. No more using a janky bedside table with textbooks stacked to get my laptop at the right height. And the little stabilizing troughs for books or my phone is a nice touch.

L’Esperance: The KICKR CORE 2 —it’s the base of my whole system. During the shoulder and winter seasons, it helps me keep my training consistent, engaging, and effective no matter the weather. The other pieces I can’t live without are the KICKR Desk and KICKR Headwind . I really wasn’t expecting them to be such a key part of the setup, but they certainly enhance the experience. Everything I need is within reach on the desk, and the Headwind offers adjustable cooling during my workouts. I don’t even need to get off the bike.

Smith: All the time! We’re not usually doing the same workout, though the flavor is often the same, but our trainers are set up in the basement on either side of our squat rack. We aim to ride at similar times, which helps with motivation and mobilizing energy to get the work done. It’s nice to have a partner in your suffering, and then we can also provide each other feedback and encouragement on form, effort, etc. We’ll often put the sound system on and turn the basement into a bit of a dance club on the trainers.

L’Esperance: It hasn’t changed significantly since focusing on endurance MTB and gravel events. However, I have refined how I use the indoor trainer. I try to do a maximum of three to four indoor sessions per week throughout the “indoor season.” I keep the sessions structured and focused and make sure the indoor trainer never becomes a grind. In the winter, I’ll also get outside for basic endurance building by running, fat-biking, hiking, and ski-touring. I love moving outside in nature as part of training, and the indoor trainer cannot fully replicate that for me, so that balance is important.

Smith: One of the major differences between XCO MTB, which we used to do, and the longer endurance-style racing we currently do is the steady, uninterrupted pressure on the pedals for extended periods of time. There’s less descending and coasting than there is in XCO, and a lot more constant pedaling at high loads. Indoor training gets rid of things like stoplights and prolonged descents, so we naturally get that steady pressure. It’s not uncommon to have fewer than two to three minutes at less than 100W (that is, fewer than two to three minutes of coasting) in an entire indoor trainer ride. This is both superefficient and very specific to the demands of our racing.

L’Esperance: The endurance off-road racing space is becoming more and more competitive, and starting quite early in the year. Events like BWR AZ, Cape Epic, and Santa Vall are in February and March, so the indoor trainer is an essential race prep tool if you live in a winter climate. The indoor trainer actually allows me to prepare better for these events because of the quality work I can get done.

Located in Atlanta, Georgia, Wahoo Fitness has a vision to be a global leader in smart fitness and training by creating a full ecosystem of software, sensors, devices, data, and performance insights for runners, cyclists, triathletes, and other competitive endurance athletes and fitness enthusiasts. title: Nvidia hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair
text:
Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affir between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy.

Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.

Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation" into the affair. The FBI is also conducting its own probe.

The firm's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (£375bn) being wiped of its stock market value since Friday.

Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom given it is the sole manufacturer of a crucial computer chip required for successfully operating AI tools.

It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials keen to win the AI race.

Alice Huang was an executive at a Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia.

The company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked.

Nvidia has also maintained the US government did not inform the firm that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern.

According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring of this year warning that the Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

Beijing has rejected claims that Jensen Huang has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China".

US President Donald Trump said Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang and that the Nvidia boss told him "I had no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed the him.

However, the relationship has drawn more political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Jensen Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing.

The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC.

The committee has the authority to subpoena Jensen Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before the committee, if deemed necessary.

When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

It added that a committee of independent directors would oversee the probe.

What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond

Joon Kim, who will lead Nvidia's investigation, is a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District and spent several years working as a government attorney focused on fraud and other criminal acts.

Wachtell is one of the largest law firms in the US and has several notable clients in the tech industry. Among them are OpenAI and Salesforce.

The investigation will likely be treated as urgent, according to sources familiar with the matter, as Jensen Huang's public image is tightly intertwined with Nvidia.

He has become a key public figure in the development on AI, arguing the technology is a "new industrial revolution" and is on par with the advent of electricity.

It is unclear, however, if Wachtell will be able to interview Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang.

A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on Tuesday when asked if Jensen Huang had retained any additional of his own legal representation amid the company investigation and the separate one launched by the FBI.

title: Velo Poll: Did the UCI Blow It in Schreiber CX Relegation?
author: ahood
text:
Marie Schreiber was stunned after she was relegated Saturday. Did the race jury make the right call? (Photo: Billy Ceusters/Getty Images)

Marie Schreiber crossed the line first at Saturday’s European cyclocross championships , but she didn’t win.

The UCI race jury relegated her after citing an irregular sprint, and everyone’s still raging about it.

Check the replay : Schreiber led out the sprint, moved slightly to her left as Lucinda Brand was sprinting beside the barriers.

The race jury didn’t like it and relegated the Luxembourg rider to second, wiping out what would have been her biggest win.

The fallout continues. Brand said she felt beaten straight up and didn’t file a formal protest. Her coach, Sven Nys, questioned the decision as well.

The Luxembourg cycling federation has posted a formal complaint, but so far, Brand is still the official winner.

Was Schreiber closing the door unfairly, or did the jury deliver a punishment that was simply too harsh?

title: Past results and wildcard invitations now define 'pro' categories at The Traka World Series events, The Rift keeps a limited number of entries open for women - Gravel Bits
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
Organisers of The Traka World Series , formerly Gravel Earth Series, announced the ranking procedures to determine overall winners for 2027, with balanced points for the top 25 riders in pro divisions at each of the seven races, and a new system for riders to earn entry into the pro category as well.

There will be no enhanced scores for individual events, which had been the case in the past at The Traka 360 and the series finale, The River. At Traka Girona and the final series stop, now The Last Dance, points will be the same as other events.

In the past, riders could compete at either The Traka 200 or The Traka 360, or both, which was rare, with more points on the line in the longer distance. This year, pro fields will be consolidated in the reworked 300km distance on May 1, which will offer points and recognise clear winners in the big tune-up before Unbound Gravel.

There are new criteria for riders to line up in the pro division for the popular Girona race, which prioritise results from last year. Riders having finished within 5% of the winning time in their gender category can race as pros. Top finish times from the year before also apply from The Traka 200, Santa Vall, and the longer distances from Ranxo Gravel, Gravel Desert and The River 160.

And at the first three series races in 2027, the same 5% margin will apply for riders to gain pro status, including a new event in late spring referred to as 'The Traka in the Americas'. Organisers added that a limited number of wild card entries would be considered, "assessed on the sporting information provided and the eligibility criteria of each application".

There will be no minimum number of events required in the series, however, athletes must start the season finale in October, The Last Dance. Once the seventh and final event has been completed, the final standings will be decided from points earned after dropping the two lowest scores in the calendar.

The final top 10 in The Traka World Series pro leaderboards, men and women, will share a €20,000 overall prize purse. At each event, the top five pro riders, men and women, will have another €8,000 on offer, with CORE4's purse double that amount.

The Rift gravel race in Iceland is officially sold out for 2027, but organisers announced a few days ago that they are keeping a limited number of entries open for women in the 200-kilometre distance. They want 200 women on the July 24 start line for the 200km distance.

Started in 2019, The Rift offers routes from 60km to 330km from Hvolsvöllur, Iceland across the rough volcanic highlands, marked by multiple icy-cold water crossings. The 200km distance is considered the main event, won last year by Anton Stensby and Haley Smith.

Registration for The Rift 200k is $320. For any rider, male or female, who wishes to compete in shorter categories - 140km or 60km - opportunities are still available to join the waitlist. The long-distance 'Abyss' event is closed.

Valley of Tears returns next year for a fourth year, March 5-6, with two days of racing in Turkey, Texas. Organisers announced they will expand the number of titles on offer for the USA Cycling Collegiate Gravel National Championships, with four stars-and-stripes jerseys up for grabs in 2027.

A star-studded elite field is expected to compete for a $45,000 prize purse, split evenly between pro women and pro men. The first payouts are at Friday's Dirt Crit presented by QTS with $10,000 for pro/open competitors. The balance is shared on Saturday for the 93-mile main event, with chunky gravel, old rail trail, sand and singletrack that passes through Caprock Canyons State Park.

In 2026, Valley of Tears hosted the inaugural nationals for collegiate riders, won by Nate Meister (Fort Lewis) and Emma Kasza-James (Midwestern State). Fort Lewis College took the team title. This year, four categories will be offered - Varsity Men, Varsity Women, Club Men and Club Women.

The event offers three ride distances - 20 miles, 50 miles and 93 miles. Registration is limited to 1,000 riders across all fields and opens with discounted rates at 7:00 a.m. CDT on December 1, 2026.

Last year, Sofia Gomez Villafane (Specialized Off-road) captured her third consecutive victory at Valley of Tears, holding off Paige Onweller (Trek Driftless), while Alexey Vermeulen (ENVE) won from a three-rider sprint among the elite men.

title: Firing a manager is often more about maintaining the illusion of control | Leander Schaerlaeckens
author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
text:
In an era of advanced analytics, deciding when to move on from a manager still seems to come down to vibes rather than logic

He’d run out of time, out of credit, out of chances.

This time of year, we live in permanent peril of hearing some version of the above proclaimed with unshakable confidence. Some soccer manager has been fired and it is universally agreed that it had to be done, that there was no alternative, that the club’s hands were tied by circumstance.

It’s all a bit weird, this broadly accepted yet totally unscientific formula for when a manager must – MUST – lose his job. It’s a sort of alchemy of vibes, and results, and the absence of other scapegoats, and the alternatives available. It’s like that old definition of hardcore pornography by a US supreme court justice: I know it when I see it.

Shall we talk about Michael Carrick now? Yes, here is where we are obliged to debate the beleaguered Manchester United manager, who has been at the helm during the Red Devils’ first dip into the relegation zone since 1986 yet somehow is also definitely not at fault. There is almost total agreement on the latter point, that United’s issues are structural and systemic and absolve Carrick of blame. Still, he’s gotta go, because what can you do, eh?

By the time you read this, he may be gone, or about to be gone , or still floating around in the liminal vapors of being emotionally, but not yet physically, gone.

He was caretaker manager and did such a good job at that free-hit, can’t-lose gig – five stars! Clean and comfortable ride! – that he was rewarded with the exact same but altogether more difficult job of being the permanent Manchester United manager.

But the discourse has shifted against Carrick. Suddenly, the exact same skillset that helped him rescue United last season, making him a poster child of club DNA and its virtues, is viewed as deficient.

Now they say Carrick is outsmarted by the other managers, overwhelmed by the volume of games. Perhaps. But his tactical mind was up to it last year. With fewer games to worry about, certainly, but also burdened with Ruben Amorim’s debris to clear away first. Amorim, of course, was the predecessor who Simply Had To Go, because he was dogmatic and would need too much time to instill his methods, after he was hired because the club must have quite liked that he was dogmatic, even though he would need considerable time to instill his methods.

Yet hanging on to a manager often works out. There’s the famous case of Sir Alex Ferguson, of course, who was installed during United’s last flirtation with relegation, 40 years ago. The early years of his reign were not always smooth: he had a poor season in 1988-89 and was reportedly a few bad results from being sacked in January 1990. But he wasn’t, and nine years later, he was knighted for his accomplishments in management and, by extension, in not being fired.

It’s true of Mikel Arteta, too, who has teetered several times in charge of Arsenal. When the now-defending champions started the 2021-22 season without winning or scoring in three matches, including a 5-0 humiliation by Manchester City. And in late 2024. And as recently as this spring, when some felt that if Arteta didn’t deliver the title at last, he ought to be replaced. Six months on, that seems unthinkable.

There’s a graphic doing the rounds on social media showing that Carrick has actually done slightly better than Arteta in his first 27 league matches in charge, although this elides the very obviously opposite trajectories they were on. All the same, Arteta got to keep going; Carrick probably won’t. Few managers these days are allowed to grow on the job, or into it. The very things Ferguson once credited for his longevity – the leeway to evolve and develop and learn from his mistakes, to rebuild and retool – are denied to the managers supposed to succeed him. Because of … reasons? The money was different back then, but the pressure wasn’t .

Instead, that predictable thing has happened where Carrick has morphed from the in-fashion manager to the one who is gently mocked. He’s no longer said to look calm and possessed of the desperately needed poise at a tumultuous club. Now, he is described as glum. It seemed an ominous portent that he should add himself to the ultra-niche lore of English managers misusing umbrellas when he promised to hold the umbrella so that he would get wet and keep everyone else at the club dry, possibly owing to an unfamiliarity with the rudiments of the technology.

Carrick isn’t alone in managerial purgatory.

Crystal Palace’s Pierre Sage: sacked but somehow not yet sacked .

Régis Le Bris: safe for now, in spite of taking newly promoted Sunderland to an astounding seventh place last season.

Newcastle’s Matthias Jaissle: medium rare, but not yet cooked.

Manchester City’s Enzo Maresca: definitely no longer the perfect successor to Pep Guardiola he was just a few weeks ago.

Fulham’s Álvaro Arbeloa and Bournemouth’s Marco Rose and Tottenham’s Roberto De Zerbi are fine now, after starting the season very not fine. That may change after any result at all. Because clubs’ decision-making on managers seems to be all just guesses and gambles. A veneer of deep deliberation is projected on to the process, because on the outside we always assume that soccer is more sophisticated than it is, but none of them really know which manager will perform in what situation, and for how long.

That’s amazing, given the advances in analytics and how much really rides on a manager’s ability to win games. Ballooning analytics departments seem to have taken teams to a place where they make far fewer mistakes in the transfer market than they used to.

Yet hiring a new manager, or firing the old one, or giving him another chance, appears to involve only marginally more design than shaking a Magic 8 Ball and seeing whether it endorses your choice.…

title: Garmin’s Latest Update Puts a Real-Time Warning on Drivers’ Dashboards
author: Josh Ross
text:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Today Garmin announced a partnership with the community-driven navigation app Waze. The connection will allow cyclists to show up on a driver’s navigation display, and it all works through the Garmin LiveTrack feature.

If you are unfamiliar, LiveTrack is a free feature built into compatible Garmin bike computers and smartwatches that lets users share their real-time location, speed and course plans with family and friends. It’s a feature that is not unique to Garmin hardware, although competitors have sometimes struggled to execute such a streamlined approach. The Garmin solution allows for a simple list of contacts who get an automatic notification every time you press start on a ride, as well as the option to send links individually.

Garmin is now expanding that usability to Waze. With this new update, that same location data is temporarily broadcast to approaching Waze users as an active icon on their screen. Simply opt in via Garmin Connect and your location will appear as a real-time, moving icon on the Waze mobile app. Drivers in the area who use Waze will see “Live Cycling Alerts” when a rider is using the Garmin integrated feature. Gai Berkovich, vice president and general manager of Waze, said, “By bringing Live Cycling Alerts to Waze, we’re giving drivers a helpful heads-up so they can slow down, stay aware and safely share the road.”

Garmin has also specified that “location sharing is temporary and session-based, and the cyclist’s personal information will not be shared or displayed in Waze.” The feature is now rolling out globally on Android and iOS. Visit the Garmin website for more information.

title: Claude chatbot maker set for $1.3tn stock market debut despite 'catastrophic' AI warning
text:
Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude chatbot, could be valued at around $1.3 trillion (£1 trillion) when it lists its shares for sale on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.

The loss-making company says it will offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each and will raise up to $64bn when it floats this month.

It would value Anthropic at between $1.1tn and $1.3tn which, although large, is below the $2tn some backers of the firm predicted in summer, according to the Financial Times.

It is floating at a volatile time for AI firms. After last week's US midterm elections, the Nasdaq fell sharply on concerns a Democrat-led Congress could slow development of AI and the buildout of data centres.

There are also wider fears over the billions of dollars being spent on AI and whether it will pay off.

In its most recent results for the six months to the end of June, Anthropic's revenues jumped to $16.2bn from $1.1bn in the same period last year.

However, its pre-tax loss jumped to $80.7bn from $12.9bn.

Fiona Cincotta, a senior market analyst at City Index, said the $64bn Anthropic wants to raise is "fairly bullish" within "the volatility [and] concerns towards AI that we've seen in sort of particularly last week".

She told Reuters: "It's showing that they are still sort of upbeat about the outlook as far as AI is concerned and that obviously that they think that the demand is going to be there."

At $1.3tn, Anthropic's possible valuation is below SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company, which listed its shares in June and was valued at nearly $1.8tn.

Anthropic is just five years old. It was co-founded in 2021 by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei along with five others - all of whom worked at OpenAI, the rival AI giant behind ChatGPT.

title: Peter Sagan’s Former Team Saved, Another Door Shut for Primož Roglič
author: ahood
text:
Peter Sagan's final team TotalEnergies will keep racing after the arrival of a new sponsor, but there's no room for Roglič. (Photo: Michael Steele/Getty Images)

TotalEnergies — the second-tier French team where Peter Sagan ended his career — is saved by the bell as teams and riders are getting nervous as 2026 winds down.

Team manager Jean-René Bernaudeau revealed Tuesday that XEFI, a French IT company, committed to three years to keep the long-running team in the peloton.

With just weeks before winter team camps, the announcement went down to the wire to meet registration deadlines and keep riders under contract.

“It’s late, there was pressure, there was anticipation, that much we understand. But today, we savor this feeling of peace and confidence all the more,” sport director Stéphane Heulot told L’Equipe .

Heulot said the team will see a mix of veterans and rising talent for 2027, mostly French, but with more international tilt in the coming season.

Is there room for Primoz Roglič , the superstar Slovenian who is still hunting for a deal? Probably not.

“I would say that today the roster is almost complete. A shock transfer? I don’t know who we could talk about today. Roglič maybe? But honestly, that’s not something we have on the table,” he said. “I don’t want to do a publicity stunt like some teams have done when they don’t actually have the means to hire him.”

The deal saves the team from the edge of oblivion. TotalEnergies confirmed the end of its long-running sponsorship with the team, but appears to be remaining in cycling with partnership with Netcompany-Ineos.

After flirting with international riders like Sagan — who raced his final two seasons with the team — and Edvald Boasson Hagen, the team pivoted back to its French roots the past few years. It won a Tour de France stage in 2024 with Antony Turgis and provided a pipeline for more French riders to start the Tour.

The team was founded in 2000 and has raced the Tour every year since.

Fans will recognize the different names over the years, from Bonjour, Brioches La Boulangère, Bouygues Télécom, Europcar, Direct Énergie, and TotalEnergies, but this has been Bernaudeau’s baby.

The late-hour save is good news for French cycling, which is facing the same problems of rising costs while trying to compete against a few elite super teams at the top of the pyramid.

Coming out of 2026, no major WorldTour teams are facing imminent closure, but there are a few teams in the lower ranks that look to be closing.

France’s St Michel-Auber93 — a modest team from a Parisian suburb that raced a few Tours over the years — is shutting down its long-running men’s that dates back to the 1990s. Management will pivot toward backing the women’s team and hope for a Tour de France Femmes invitation in 2027.

Hitec Products, a women’s Norwegian Continental team, confirmed its shutting down at the end of this season, citing difficulties to get into major races.

Two more second-tier men’s teams that played out-sized roles are also shutting at the end of 2026.

Team Flanders-Baloise, with its DNA dating back to the 1990s, is folding after the Flemish government withdrew key public funding. Long a fixture in the classics, the team was a “talent farm” for budding Belgian riders to make the jump to the WorldTour.

Thomas De Gendt, Sep Vanmarcke, Victor Campenaerts, Oliver Naesen, and Yves Lampaert all did stints with the team over the years.

Kern Pharma, the Spanish ProTeam since 2020, is also restructuring for 2027 after the longtime pharmaceutical company did not extend its sponsorship. Riders like Pablo Castrillo, Roger Adrìa and Raúl García Pierna all raced on the team before bouncing to the WorldTour.

Riders have been told they’re free to find new teams and the squad could continue at a lower level next season.

The Slovenian showed up this week in Taiwan, but there’s still no confirmed team for the four-time Vuelta a España champion.

The 37-year-old parted ways with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe after three season, and it remains uncertain if there will be a closing-hour deal.

Contract talks with several teams, including Visma-Lease a Bike, Unibet Rose Rockets, Pinarello-Q36.5, and Lotto-Intermarché, have all apparently collapsed.

Roglič — once of cycling’s “Big Four” — remains ambivalent about his future and even whether he wants to continue racing.

He still finished second at the Vuelta a España and earned nearly 1,000 UCI points in 2026, which would be valuable to teams chasing a WorldTour license, but a reported $2 million asking price might have to come down if he wants to find a deal this late in the season.

title: Mauricio Pochettino interested in leaving USMNT job for Manchester United
author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer and Jamie Jackson
text:
Coach’s contract has release clause of about $10m

United expected to sack Michael Carrick after awful start

US men’s national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino is interested in a move to Manchester United, multiple sources told the Guardian, with those same sources characterizing the interest as mutual.

United are expected to sack their head coach, Michael Carrick, after a disastrous start to their season which leaves them at risk of relegation from the Premier League, their worst opening to a campaign in four decades.

Securing Pochettino’s services is far from simple or inexpensive. The Argentinian’s contract contains a release clause in the neighborhood of $10m (£7.5m), multiple sources familiar with the deal told the Guardian this week, a figure that grows should United choose to retain Pochettino’s staff, including his longtime assistant and confidant Jesús Pérez, who has worked with Pochettino for 16 years. The Athletic first reported the details of Pochettino’s buyout.

Pochettino was brought on by the US in 2024 and guided the USMNT to a last-16 finish at the 2026 World Cup , by most accounts a disappointment. US Soccer brought him back through 2030 , with both sides expressing a mutual belief and commitment towards not only brightening the fortunes of the US men but also overhauling the federation’s approach towards youth development.

“Every time we sign a contract, it’s to go to the last day of the contract,” Pochettino told reporters after his contract renewal. “If we sign a four-year contract, we need to think to arrive there. And we signed the contract because we really believe that we are going to be four years there. Because if not, it’s bad. If we don’t believe in that process, if we don’t believe in that journey, why sign [for] four years? Only to be sure that we are going to receive a salary at the end of the month? That is not nice. title: Liberty Media founder sells voting power of F1's parent company
author: Samarth Kanal
text:
Liberty Media founder and ex-chairman John Malone has sold his significant voting power in Formula 1's parent company.

Malone founded Liberty Media in 1991 and stepped down as chairman of the board in 2026, nine years after Liberty Media acquired F1 for $4.6billion USD (£3.4bn).

Malone was the most significant voting shareholder of Liberty Media until early November 2026 when Liberty Media announced that it had purchased Malone's 'high-vote' stock and exchanged it for 'low-vote' stock, essentially diluting Malone's voting power from around 48% to 3%.

Liberty Media purchased the high-vote stock after Malone received "a number of unsolicited offers from third parties" to acquire it.

The transaction effectively eliminates the transfer of Malone's voting power to a third party and strengthens Liberty Media shareholders' power in voting matters - such as a sale of F1.

In 2025, Malone said on the Opening Bid Unfiltered finance podcast that Liberty would be open to a sale of F1 - with the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund (PIF) among F1's then-touted suitors.

He said F1 "has an exceptionally good economic structure", adding: "It's a public company. If somebody gets carried away, and they want to buy it, and they're willing to pay more for it than the board thinks that they can deliver to the shareholders, then we would sell it. That's the bottom line."

Liberty Media president and CEO Derek Chang said during the company's Q3 earnings call that Malone "controlled a significant set of votes with a relatively low economic interest".

He explained that Liberty Media's purchase of the voting shares "helps us effectively control our own destiny forward".

There is no indication that Liberty Media is considering a sale of F1 in 2026.

Chang added: "We're still focused primarily on growing the businesses that we have. And as we stated previously, sort of investing behind those businesses and growth plans that they have is probably the biggest priority as we think about other forms of capital allocation."

The net worth of F1 sits at nearly $28bn as of November 2026, with the average value of an F1 team having reached $3.6bn in 2025 according to Forbes.

In 2025, Liberty Media completed its acquisition of an 84% stake in MotoGP commercial rights holder Dorna for around $3.3bn or €3.02bn.

title: Kim Kardashian's Skims offers refunds for $148 advent calendar after backlash
text:
Kim Kardashian's Skims is offering customers refunds for its $148 (£110) advent calendar which has been widely criticised on social media.

The accessories advent calendar promised "twelve days of fun surprises" but has been mocked online for the quality of its contents, such as hair clips and keychains, with some comparing them to something you would find down the back of a sofa.

A spokesperson for Skims has told a number of media outlets "for some, the calendar didn't meet expectations" and the company has "personally contacted every customer" to offer a full refund or credit to put towards other products".

The BBC has contacted Skims for comment.

The shapewear and clothing business was co-founded by Kardashian in 2019 and has made the reality TV star a billionaire, according to Forbes magazine.

Skims was valued at $5bn in 2025 when it raised millions of dollars in new funding.

One account on TikTok called spicychathouse compared the contents of the calendar to things "my cat collects from around my house". Another account said it looked like "a bunch of stuff that Kim Kardashian was emptying out of her bedside table".

A number of accounts showed people cleaning out their own sofas and claiming they had accidentally created the Skims advent calendar.

"It is really interesting to see this kind of backlash," said Kate Vlietstra, senior director of food and drink at market research analyst Mintel.

"It is something we have been seeing a bit more in recent years, particularly with the trend for unboxing on social media," she said,

"It means that, inevitably, if people are not feeling they're getting the value that they have hoped for from the advent calendar...they've purchased, then yes, there is going to be a backlash."

Advent calendars remain popular, according to Helen Wing, head of innovation at market research company Ipsos though she said that "the buzz around them has reduced a little bit".

She said according to Ipsos research, people are willing to pay a bit more for an advent calendar but the contents have to justify the price tag.

Using a £285 advent calendar sold by Liberty as an example, Wing said the upmarket department story is "very open about the value of the contents".

"They will say there is over £1,000 worth of content," she said. "If you've got that reassurance when you're making the purchase, particularly if it is for a gift, then it is important to have some faith that the contents are actually going to be worth the money that you're paying."

What is the most money you’ve spent on an advent calendar, and was it worth it? Let us know.

Room to Go Long: Belgian Waffle Ride Finds Its Ultra in Montana
author: Kelly Matkovich
text:
Riders trace a ribbon of road through Montana’s open ranchlands, dwarfed by the landscape surrounding them. (Photo: ROB WESSELS)

Stella Hobbs had a practical response to the cold and rain at the start of the 2026 Belgian Waffle Ride Montana: make everybody ride harder.

“Between my chattering teeth and numb toes, I decided there was only one solution,” she wrote afterward. “As soon as the neutral ended, I was going to make the race hard. It was time to create some heat.”

The Montana native went to work on the early climbs, taking Cécile Lejeune with her. Across the Gallatin Valley, the weather was conducting several different experiments. Some riders found sunshine. Others rode through passing showers. The moisture settled the dust, the clouds moved across the hills, and the roads kept drawing people farther into a landscape that appeared to have considerably more riding available than we had put on the menu.

Hobbs would win her second consecutive BWR Montana, averaging 20.5 mph across 106 miles. The leading five men averaged more than 22 mph before Hayden Christian claimed a fiercely contested finish. It was the fastest Belgian Waffle Ride we had ever produced. Five riders within a second or two.

For those of us putting it on, Montana was also answering a question we had been asking for years.

For my partners, Phil Tinstman and Randall Coxworth, and me, that question predates our arrival in Bozeman. Belgian Waffle Ride enters its 16th year in 2027, and throughout those years of producing events across North America, we have wanted to create an ultra-distance course.

We have certainly inflicted some substantial days on people. The longest BWR reached 146 miles. Over time, the full-distance Waffle has settled closer to 110 miles, which remains a perfectly respectable distance to spend reconsidering your tire choice.

But the three of us have an affection for going longer. Randall and Phil are Race Across America record holders. I am a Race Across the West record holder. We have spent plenty of time discovering what happens when a ride outlasts your fresh legs, your initial enthusiasm and several entirely reasonable opportunities to stop.

We love that experience. We have wanted to share it through BWR.

At the venues we have been fortunate enough to work with, however, we could never get the ultra course to come together. Creating a worthwhile 200-mile race requires more than dragging a line farther across a map. The terrain has to sustain the adventure. The connections have to work. The extra miles need to earn their place.

In and north of town, the riding opens into broad valleys, rolling ranchlands, gravel climbs and stretches of backcountry that make you curious about what lies beyond the next ridge. From one hillside, you can watch a road work its way across another. A distant group becomes a moving speck. The scale changes your understanding of how much country a bicycle can carry you through.

Under your tires, the experience keeps changing, too. Fast stretches encourage cooperation and occasionally poor judgment. Rougher ground rewards attention. Climbs interrupt conversations that everyone had been enjoying. Pavement connects the pieces, giving riders a chance to find a rhythm before the next change of surface.

This is what we call Unroad: following the character of a place across the surfaces that make it interesting.

Our first two Montana editions gave us the opportunity to build Waffle, Wafer and Wanna courses worthy of that landscape. Going into our third year, we are adding the serving we have been talking about all along.

Named for Belgium’s largest style of waffle, the new 200-plus-mile ultra-distance race will anchor Belgian Waffle Ride Montana , taking place September 17–18, 2027, in Bozeman . It will also host the 2027 WUCA North American Gravel Ultra-Distance Championships , the first official continental gravel ultra-distance championship sanctioned by the World UltraCycling Association .

A Flemish portion with Montana proportions. We suggest arriving hungry.

For Randall, Phil and me, the championship brings together two parts of our cycling lives that we have spent years trying to connect. We get to take the patience, preparation and persistence we love about ultra riding and bring them into a BWR course with room to unfold.

“We’ve always believed a great bike race should ask more of you than how hard you can pedal,” I said when we announced the championship. “Montana gives us the landscape to ask all sorts of decidedly difficult questions.”

Over 200-plus miles, those questions become increasingly personal.

How much effort can you afford on this climb? Have you been eating according to your plan, or waiting for your body to lodge a formal complaint? Can you keep choosing good lines when your hands are tired? Can you let a difficult stretch pass without deciding it represents the remainder of your life?

The distance gives decisions time to accumulate. A restrained first hour can become a gift much later. An unnecessary acceleration can acquire interest. Another rider’s company can change the complexion of an afternoon.

Montana gives those experiences a spectacular setting. The views stretch well beyond the wheel ahead, and the changing terrain keeps you involved in the ride. There is a lot to take in, even when you are busy negotiating with yourself.

The Brussels Waffle will offer continental titles and custom WUCA champion jerseys to the overall male and female winners and to male and female winners in designated age groups. Riders across generations will have the opportunity to chase championship honors, with final eligibility, category rules and membership requirements published alongside the official event information.…

title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
author: Associated Press at the Rafah crossing
text:
Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent

Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.

The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.

“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine . I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.

Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.

Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.

At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.

Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.

The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.

The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

title: Sales of tinned food and bottled water jump after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
text:
Sales of essential goods such as bottled water and canned food soared in the 10 days following the launch of the government's "Be Ready" emergency preparedness campaign on 22 October, research indicates.

Hand sanitiser sales were up 83%, sales of bottled water rose 67% and tinned and jarred goods climbed 37%, according to data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator.

The government's public awareness campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.

However, Worldpanel said that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.

The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.

Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.

After the campaign launch, the equivalent of an extra 400,000 people per day bought tinned meat, Worldpanel said, although the typical amount remained at 500g, which suggests a gradual stocking-up.

"Shoppers clearly took notice of the 'Be Ready' campaign, but this wasn't panic buying, with less than a third of households buying bottled water in October," said Fraser McKevitt, head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel by Numerator.

"Growth came from more people adding the recommended items on the government's checklist to their weekly shop, not from shoppers piling their trolleys high, which is very much in line with what the government wanted households to do," he said.

Sales of tinned and jarred goods rose from £58.2m in the 10 days to 2 November 2025 to £79.5m over the same period in 2026.

Bottled water sales jumped from £13.6m to £22.8m compared with a year earlier and hand sanitiser sales climbed from £497,000 to £908,000.

Further evidence of stockpiling came from food firm Princes on Tuesday, which said demand for tinned tuna, meat and vegetables had risen following the government's campaign.

Princes interim chief executive Giuseppe Mastrolia said the jump in demand "further reinforces the relevance of our core categories in providing affordable, nutritious and convenient food solutions".

The "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need - for example, bottled water, and long-life food that doesn't need to be kept in the fridge such as dried fruit and nuts.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments".

Disaster recovery expert Lucy Easthope previously told the BBC that the UK was playing "massive catch up" to other European nations in terms of preparedness.

These include France, Germany Denmark, Sweden, and Norway.

A number of experts have been calling for the UK to put more emphasis on food security, with some arguing that the government itself should take responsibility for food stockpiling, rather than individual households.

In October, a group of more than 180 experts signed an open letter , external to Burnham and first secretary of state Louise Haigh calling for local authorities to have a duty to prevent and respond to food supply emergencies.

They pointed out that a government survey found that 29% of people in the UK could not afford to keep a few days worth of food in the house.

title: Formula 1 to finish season in Middle East
text:
Formula 1 has told the Imola circuit in Italy that it will not be required as a back-up for the two end-of-season races in the Middle East.

The sport is pressing ahead with plans to hold the two events in Qatar on 27-29 November and Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates on 4-6 December, despite the ongoing conflict between the United States/Israel and Iran.

Imola had been asked to prepare for a potential grand prix on the Abu Dhabi dates if the two Middle Eastern races could not go ahead.

Imola was asked on Tuesday to stand down preparations - but F1 says that if the situation in the Middle East deteriorates it is still prepared to cancel the two races.

Earlier in the season, races in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain, both of which had been scheduled for April, were cancelled and delayed respectively following the outbreak of the United States and Israel's war with Iran.

The Bahrain Grand Prix was eventually held at Malaysia's Sepang circuit in October.

"If the situation develops negatively in the coming weeks before the events in the Middle East, we will not hesitate to do the right thing and the safety of everyone will always be the priority," an F1 spokesperson said on Tuesday.

F1 says the decision to press ahead with Qatar and Abu Dhabi, which was always the default option, has been taken because the situation in the two countries has not "negatively developed" in recent months.

Travel advice from governments still allows travel, insurance is valid, events are taking place and business has returned to a normal level in both countries, it said, adding that the teams are all supportive of concluding the season as planned.

A MotoGP race was held in Qatar last weekend. That sport is owned by the same US group that owns F1.

Despite the decision, a number of senior figures in F1 have expressed disquiet to BBC Sport about the idea of going to the Middle East for the races, as both are close to areas in the Straight of Hormuz where missile strikes are still taking place.

And Saudi Arabia continues to be the target of attacks from Houthi rebels in Yemen.

Several events in Saudi Arabia, which borders Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, have been cancelled or postponed in recent weeks following those attacks.

However, there is recognition that F1 faces a difficult decision. The two countries pay large fees for their events, and both are heavily ingrained in the fabric of the sports as sponsors and investors.

The Qatari sovereign investment fund, for example, is a part owner of the Audi team, and Abu Dhabi is the same for McLaren.

US inflation higher than expected in October - here's what is happening with prices
text:
US inflation rose at a faster-than-expected pace in October, according to official figures.

Prices rose by 0.4% in the month, which was lower than the 0.6% increase in September.

However, analysts had expected prices to rise by 0.3%, and the higher-than-expected pace could add to arguments for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its next meeting in December.

The new figures come a week after the midterm elections which were fought over cost-of-living pressures across the US.

Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increases over time.

For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.

Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).

It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.

The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.

There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.

If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.

Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.

Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.

Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel, but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.

Over the month of October, prices rose by 0.4%, driven by increases in housing, food and energy costs.

However, the pace of energy price rises, at 0.7% in October, was much lower than the 5.2% increase seen in September.

While the Bureau of Labor Statistics would normally provide figures for the 12-month change in prices, it did not collect data in October 2025 so it could not provide that estimate.

For the 12 months to September, inflation was 3.7%.

The US Federal Reserve has a target for keeping annual inflation at 2%.

When inflation is too high the Fed tends to raise interest rates in order to encourage people and businesses to save more and spend less money in the hope this will slow price rises.

While there was no annual figure published for inflation this month, analysts say the fact inflation was higher in October than expected increases the chance of an interest rate rise at the Fed's December meeting.

Federal Reserve governor Chirstopher Waller, who spoke before the latest inflation figures were published, also suggested he was leaning towards a rate increase in December even if October's figures were slower than expected.

US interest rates held steady and economy grows - what it means for you

Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.

While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.

Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.

In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.

Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.

Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.

While inflation is currently above where the Federal Reserve would like it has been much higher in previous years.

During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up.

Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel.

Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%.

It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.

A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.

Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.

Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect price rises to slow further, or to fall. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.

The value of social security benefits is changed to largely keep up with inflation, protecting people's ability to purchase their usual goods and services through the cost-of-living adjustment.

Shortly after September's inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by a similar amount - 3.6% - in 2027.

The administration said that the 3.6% rise will mean an average retirement benefit increase of $75 a month.…

You asked, we answered: Our Labs experts on wind tunnel testing, reverse mullet wheels, our ultimate Roubaix setups and more – AskCN
author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
text:
Welcome to the first edition of Ask CN, a new AMA-style series on where our readers get the chance to put their questions to us, our columnists, and more.

For the inaugural episode, we're shining a light on CN Labs, the longstanding series of wind tunnel tests, rolling resistance tests and other empirical inquisitions into bikes, gear and industry trends.

Over the course of the past week, subscribers, readers and followers have been submitting questions to Josh, Will and Tom - the CN tech team responsible for the aforementioned tests. Today, subscribers alone will get to read their answers.

So whether you're curious about the technical details of our wind tunnel protocol, want to know what future tests we have in mind, or even the bike we'd choose for Roubaix, you'll find it below.

And if you're not yet subscribed, then there's no better time to join our ever-growing community that gets unlimited access to all our industry-leading tests, expert tech insight, comprehensive race coverage, and plenty of subscriber-exclusive articles, like our AskCN Q&As!

Do you have a standard setup or a standard bike on which you calibrate your equipment in order to make sure you can compare results from different campaigns? (Kleinkaro)

Start with an easy one… we do!

We have my old Trek Emonda ALR, a bike that I bought in around 2016 when I worked at a bike shop. It spent a couple of years untouched in my garage and was eventually donated to the CN Labs cause in 2024. Nowadays it lives in the office store and remains unchanged between tests so that we can use it as a 'baseline' to compare against every time we test other bikes.

I trusted this was a solid theory, but we verified it in 2025 when we did our 12 aero bikes test . We not only took along the Emonda, but also the Scott Foil we'd also tested in 2024 as a second 'baseline'.

Using the same protocols, both bikes were around six watts faster than the previous year. If we didn't take a baseline at all, we'd have just concluded that everything tested in 2025 was a similar amount (six watts) faster than the bikes we tested in 2024, even if they were actually equivalent.

The difference between the two baselines (the Foil was around 35 watts faster) changed by just 0.65w across the two tests.

Do we know how much difference modern aero clothing (aero fabrics, speed suits, aero socks etc..) makes to rider speed/power compared to the rather looser, less technical fabrics of clothing from (even the not-so-distant) past? (Bernard the Badger)

The big caveat is that clothing is massively rider dependent, so the actual savings are to be taken with a pinch of salt, but in 2025, we got hold of an outfit at each price point from Kalas, and tested how they varied.

We had the entry-level bibs and jersey, the next tier up, a road skinsuit, a time trial skinsuit, and a double-layered super-suit designed for Olympic athletes. We also threw in some extra aero accessories too.

We found 18 watts between the fastest and slowest options, but perhaps most interesting was that there was as much variance between the different high end options as there was between cheap and expensive. This, we believe, is because when you get into the high-end options, fabric choice is tailored to speed.

When will you test the new Orca Aero and SL9? Also, any plans to test TT bikes too? Or skinsuits? (flowerforalgernon)

Both of those bikes are conversations in progress. I have an SL9 here for review, but it's not in the correct size for fair wind tunnel testing.

As for TT bikes, it's not something we've got in the pipeline for now, but it's not off the table for next year.

Skinsuits, aside from testing the difference across price points mentioned above, we've not done a skinsuit head-to-head because the results are so rider-, position-, and speed-dependent. We'd either need to do it as a bit of fun, knowing the results aren't super helpful to our readers, or do it using multiple different riders, of different genders and sizes, across a load of different speeds. That's probably more than a single day in the tunnel, which isn't a dealbreaker, but I think there are higher-priority tests that we should do first.

I’d really like to know the aero impacts of a mullet setup, like the Factor Elara, 64 up front and 46 in the rear. Does that combo give the best aero and weight setup? I currently run a Zipp XPLR up front and a 650b in the rear on my Cannondale Topstone gravel setup for tyre clearance, but I don’t notice any aero penalty with the 650b in the rear. Does the wind tunnel have anything to say? (Nathan W Ramsey, via email)

You won't believe me, but we planned to do this before aero mullets were cool.

Back in 2024, when we ran our second (of three so far) aero road wheel group test , we took along some Zipp 808s and 404s. We planned to test them as sold, then run some mullet / reverse mullet tests. Sadly, we ran out of time that day and haven't come back to the idea since.

I'll definitely add this idea back onto the list, though.

For some added context, the closest we've come to your setup is running different tyre widths front and rear. Interestingly, a 38mm front with 2.0 rear is 1.1% slower than a 2.0 front and 38mm rear (on 700c Hunt CGR40 wheels, tested as a bike only using an Allied Able frame). This was done in connection with our gravel tyre width test .

Would love to see a tunnel review of the Cervélo Aspero-5, which is curiously missing from the stable of gravel bikes tested (toadpalmer)

We tried for our gravel bike shoot out back in May. Cervélo promised a bike, but then went quiet on us, and it never showed. I think our contact at PON was juggling a few Cannondale-related things at the time, but it's definitely on the radar for the future.

The Áspero-5 is a different beast from bikes like the Crux and the Elara though, which each offer 10mm+ more tyre clearance, so that should factor into buying decisions.

How about a handlebar showdown? As this is a leading edge, what about exposed cables versus internal routing for the same bars / one piece vs. aero bar and stem etc. It seems like this could be a good place to find some speed without changing one's whole bike (older frames unite LOL) (btlrck)

Can you test against a pre-aero bike from around 2016? E.g. Focus Izalco Max, then ridden by Team AG2R. Some of us are stuck with bikes from that era. I am doing some early research on a new race bike, so I'd like to know how much I am gaining with a new aero bike both on the flat and on climbs. And please always include the weight of the bikes, including the pedals. Thanks. (brookelazich)

I've combined these two questions because my answer to both leads down a similar path...

On the handlebar suggestion, I've steered clear so far because new bikes are invariably sold with proprietary one-piece cockpits, and so fewer and fewer new bikes are customisable in this way. However, I do appreciate that it ignores not only older frames, but the more budget end of the spectrum too.

As for the suggestion of testing a couple of older race bikes as a means to benchmark their performance in the wider standings, this is something I'm keen to try to make happen in 2027.

And to combine the answers into one thread, what could work well is taking a couple of old bikes. Focus Izalco Max, SuperSix Evo 3, Venge Vias(!?), and seeing how much we can close the gap to a modern bike. This probably won't happen very quickly, because we have a few other big projects in early 2027 to focus on (more on this soon), but it's on the list.

As for the pedals, we weigh without, as we don't know whether our readers are using Shimano, Look, Speedplay etc.

Would a 35mm tyre fitted to a rim optimised for 35mm tyres be as aero as a 28mm tyre on a rim optimised for 28mm tyres? (tc_fair_weather_rides)

Why are wider tyres more aerodynamic? (Cycle Tech Ireland)

Another duo of questions combined here, as they sort of ask the same thing.

To answer the first question: in our testing, they're not. They might be faster, but with everything else kept equal, they're slower.

To answer the second: it's a simple no when querying aero alone, but complicated when you try to solve for speed.

With all else equal, a narrower 28mm setup will be more aerodynamic when both are optimised for their respective tyre widths. A bigger tyre on a bigger rim has a larger frontal area – the A in the CdA equation.

To give some data to answer this, here's a graph.

As tyre width grows, so does aero drag. A 32mm tyre on the Zipp 303 XPLR wheel is faster than a 28mm tyre on the Hunt CGR 40, but this will mostly be because the Zipp wheel is 14mm deeper.

Remember, though, speed isn't only made up of aerodynamics. I implore you to read our test on 40mm tyres , as we tackled this question fairly head-on. On rougher surfaces, a 35mm tyre is 13 watts faster (per tyre) than a 28mm tyre. When we swapped to a different rim optimised for wider tyres, that saving grew to around 55w per tyre.

However, on smooth tarmac, the benefit of going wider was actually negative. Rolling resistance didn't change with any significance, and the aero got marginally worse.

So the real trade-off is aero versus rolling resistance on the surface you ride, plus a little bit of weight, cornering and acceleration peppered into the equation too. And you'll probably find that the lower tyre pressure of wider tyres means more comfort, better grip, and less chance of a puncture too.

In your wind tunnel tests, why do you take the seven different angles in such a narrow band? Why not 45 degrees, or at least 30 degrees, along with straight, 10, 20...? (Kelly Wilde)

This is down to what yaw angles you're actually likely to experience when riding. Since there isn't one predominant wind direction the world over (i.e., it blows in all directions, and we travel in all directions), we can agree that the most common wind you'll face when cycling is the air that you ride through, equivalent, therefore, to the speed you travel. And since you always travel forwards on a bike, if there were no ambient wind at all, you'd experience a 0° yaw (as is common in a velodrome).

But even if the wind is coming at you from 90° to the right, the actual experienced yaw angle will be less than this, because you're creating your own headwind by moving through air.

There are a few mathematical models that have calculated - in extreme detail - the likelihood of experiencing any given wind angle at any given time, taking into account ambient wind conditions, average riding speeds and so on.

To solve for watts, we calculate a weighted average based on the weightings supplied by one of these mathematical models.

The models all create a bell curve that centres around 0°, and in all cases, the probability of experiencing anything beyond 15° on either side is so small that it doesn't make any difference to the results when we calculate that average, and thus it would be a waste of time to test it.

Now that you know all the data on rolling resistance and aero, what would you spec as the ultimate Roubaix bike for a normal rider? (itcanalwaysbelouder)

This one felt like a good question to pose to the whole team, so you'll find individualised responses below, starting with Tom Wieckowski, who rode the Roubaix Sportive in 2024.

Next up is Will Jones, who has fronted the Cyclingnews Tech YouTube channel since its launch in Spring, during which time he's ridden and reviewed over two dozen flagship race bikes.

And finally, me (Josh Croxton).

What's more aero: Moustache or clean-shaven? (Will Strickson)

To wrap up with a silly one... this question comes from Will Strickson, the Web Editor over at our most hated mortal enemies at Cyclist Magazine.…

Hand injury from crash on way to Euros bronze forces Ceylin del Carmen Alvarado out of upcoming cyclo-cross races
author: Owen Rogers
text:
A late crash during Saturday’s UEC European Cyclo-cross Championships not only prevented Ceylin del Carmen Alvarado from fighting for the win, but has forced the Fenix-Premier Tech rider out of this week's racing.

Alvarado had been in a with a shout of winning the elite women’s race in Zeddam on Saturday, but was gapped on the final ascent of the punishing 99-step run up. Then, while battling to return to the leading duo of Marie Schreiber and Lucinda Brand, she crashed, injuring her hand.

After the crash Alvarado could be seen shaking the injured hand, and by the time she crossed the line in third place, she was unable to hold the handlebars.

Medical examinations since the incident have revealed Alvarado had sustained a ligament tear to her right thumb, and a date for her return to competition is uncertain.

"She will wear a custom-made brace, and her return to cyclocross racing will depend on how her recovery progresses. We wish her a speedy recovery!" read a post on both Alvarado's and her team's Instagram account.

Alvarado had been scheduled to race this Wednesday, November 11, at the third round of the Superprestige at Niel , but that is now out of the question, with this weekend’s Merksplas round and the X2O Trofee race at Hamme-Zogge also looking unlikely.

With Alvarado out of contention following her crash, the race was notable for the controversial relegation of Luxembourgish rider Marie Schreiber. Though she crossed the line in first place, the victory was awarded to Brand after Schreiber's sprint was judged as irregular, the 23-year-old later accusing the commissaires of stealing the biggest moment of her career .

Alvarado is one of the sport’s leading lights and has won almost every honour in the sport. She is the current Dutch national champion and won both the World and European Championships in 2020, as well as the season-long World Cup in 2024. She is yet to hit the heights this season, though her third place at the Euros was an indication she was progressing towards her best form.

title: Disgraced former leader Sheikh Hasina plans return to Bangladesh from exile
author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi
text:
Hasina fled to India in 2024 after mass uprising. She faces death penalty upon return

Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister of Bangladesh applied for a fresh passport this week.

Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule. She fled over the border to India, where she has since been allowed to live freely in Delhi.

Last November, a tribunal in Bangladesh found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death over her deadly crackdown on a student uprising that left an estimated 1,400 people dead.

Her return to Bangladesh is likely to be disruptive for the country where Hasina’s party, Awami League, is still banned and thousands of its members are in jail. Should she be allowed to return, she is likely to be arrested immediately.

Hasina first raised the prospect of going back to Bangladesh in August. Speaking to the Guardian this week, several exiled Awami League leaders also living in India confirmed that Hasina was serious and “confident” about returning by next month. They confirmed that several other party figures had returned to the country in anticipation.

On Monday, a UK lawyer acting on behalf of Hasina, wrote to the Bangladesh high commission requesting a new passport and national identity card to be issued “in a timely fashion”, in a letter seen by the Guardian.

“The reason our leader Sheikh Hasina has applied for a passport is that she genuinely wants to return,” said a party leader based in the Indian city of Kolkata, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he is not authorised to speak to the media on the party’s behalf.

Hasina has rejected the charges of mass murder and crimes against humanity and claimed the tribunal who convicted her was illegitimate. “She is confident about her return, which is why she has applied for a new passport and a national identity card. If the authorities do not issue her a passport, she will apply for a travel pass to make her return to Bangladesh possible,” said the Awami League leader.

Since Hasina’s conviction, Bangladesh government has put pressure on the Indian authorities to extradite the former prime minister. However, the Indian government – which was very close to Hasina while she was in power – has ignored the demands, straining ties between the two countries.

This week, the Bangladesh government have said that as a “terrorist”, Hasina will only be allowed to return under an “acceptable prisoner exchange” under the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty. The chief prosecutor of the tribunal who sentenced Hasina condemned her announcement to return as a “nothing but a political stunt”.

Despite her conviction and the banning of her party, Hasina still commands significant popularity among the thousands of Awami League cadre still in Bangladesh, many who have been driven underground.

Analysts believe her decision to return, despite the risk of arrest, is driven by an attempt to revive her support base and destabilise the newly-elected government, led by prime minister Tarique Rahman. They were brought to power after in February in Bangladesh’s first democratic election in decades.

Since then, the government has struggled with inflation and recent protests that shut down garment factories, which Awami League hopes to use to its political advantage.

Another Awami League leader said all those in exile intended to follow Hasina back to Bangladesh, despite the threat of arrest and jail. Many of those who were close to Hasina over her 15 years in power have faced severe criminal charges since the fall of her government and have been given lengthy prison sentences in absentia.

“All of us are planning to go back. Some of us have been sentenced in absentia by kangaroo courts, and we know we will be jailed. But we are ready to face the consequences and return to our own people. We will fight this politically,” said the senior leader, who is also based in India.

Some senior party figures have already gone back in recent months, including former MP Mustaque Ahmed Ruhi. Ruhi was immediately arrested by police after returning in September and faces prosecution over an alleged murder committed during the 2024 uprising.

“There are serious threats and dangers, but our cadres and leaders are confident and prepared to return to our people,” the leader said.

During their years in exile, Awami League leaders have continued to meet in Kolkata, where many of them are living, and are routinely summoned to Delhi to meet Hasina.

Speaking over email this week, Hasina told the Associated Press she affirmed her decision to go back. “If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people,” she said.

title: Tour Down Under announces former Giro winner Jai Hindley as first headline starter for 2027
author: James Moultrie
text:
There are just 70 days to go until WorldTour racing resumes at the Tour Down Under in Australia, but as the anticipation builds for the 2027 season, the first big-name rider on the start list has already been announced: former Giro d'Italia winner Jai Hindley .

It will mark 10 years since he made his debut riding for the national team UniSA-Australia at the Tour Down Under, and will be his first start since 2023. Despite his GC talents, Hindley has never won his home race, with overall results of 16th, 18th, 18th, and 25th from his four appearances, also taking the start in 2019 and 2020.

The 30-year-old will lead Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe in South Australia, having extended his contract with the German team through 2028 back in July. Also already confirmed alongside him will be New Zealand teammate Laurence Pithie, a former Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race winner making his fifth appearance in a row.

"I haven’t raced the Tour Down Under since 2023, so I’m really looking forward to returning," said Hindley. "It’s a great way to kick off the season, racing in the Australian summer and on home roads in front of the Aussie fans.

"The support for the Australian riders is always fantastic, and there’s such a great atmosphere around the race. It’s always a fun event to be part of, and I’m excited to get the 2027 season under way with what I’m sure will be a strong team."

Racing at the men's Tour Down Under will kick off on January 19 in Henley Beach, with six days of action via the Mount Lofty, Corkscrew Road, and Willunga Hill climbs set to decide the next Ochre jersey.

If Vine returns to defend the jersey, he will be one of the heavy favourites alongside Hindley. Despite his lack of a GC win or podium in the TDU, the latter had a stellar 2026 season for Red Bull, riding to a third-place finish overall at the Giro d'Italia, and taking 15th on GC at the Tour de France while supporting overall runner-up Remco Evenepoel.

"We are thrilled to welcome Jai back to the Santos Tour Down Under and I’m sure all cycling fans will be excited to watch him in action on South Australian roads," said race director Stuart O'Grady.

"He holds a significant place in Australian cycling history as a Grand Tour winner, and at the age of 30 he remains in the prime of his career so we are getting to see the best of him. The course suits his characteristics with his all-round ability complemented nicely by his ability to climb with the best in the peloton.

"I’m sure Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe will again field a strong team to open the UCI WorldTour season, and having Jai here along with New Zealander Laurence Pithie brings some real quality to the peloton."

It will be a history-making edition of the Tour Down Under, as the first-ever WorldTour race to hold men’s and women’s racing over the same distance on the same days. After the first three days of action in the men's event, the women's will run concurrently from January 22-24 across three identical routes from Glenelg to Victor Harbor, Christies Beach to Willunga Hill, and Norwood to Stirling.
